title: The Allosteric Blindspot: Phenotype Transfer Across Computational Design, Biological Contexts, Cell-Free Systems, and Biosensor Deployment
content: Allosteric transcription factor (aTF) biosensors connect molecular recognition to programmable biological and analytical outputs, but performance measured in one implementation context does not necessarily persist after transfer. This review frames that problem as the Allosteric Blindspot and evaluates translation as a measurable change in phenotype across computational design, biological systems, cell-free reactions, physical devices, and complex sample matrices. A curated evidence base of 120 references was examined, with 117 records forming the locked audited corpus. Predictive Fidelity, Context Transfer Fidelity, Intervention or Rescue, and Deployment Evidence were analyzed as distinct evidence classes. Seven matched or near-matched context comparisons were suitable for primary quantitative analysis and showed improved, degraded, and essentially preserved phenotypes. No matched cell-free-to-device comparison was identified. The synthesis shows that translation depends on interacting molecular, genetic, biochemical, matrix, and transduction variables and argues for treating transferability as an explicit design parameter rather than an assumed property of a biosensor.
